text_fidelity_a:
Graber Guardian 3 Bike Trunk Rack I did not realize that this would not fit my car. I have a 2006 Toyota Camry Solara Convertible and the box says it will not fit years 1993 to 2008. Nevertheless, I decided to see for myself. Due to the way the bike rack is configured, the top bar almost comes off the trunk. As a result, there would be room for only one bike as the track adjusts back and forth depending on how tight it has to be cinched (based on the car model, of course). There are two provided clips that go through the holes to keep the track from sliding after the correct length is reached.

I then wanted to try this on my boyfriend's car which is a 2010 Honda Accord and it also will not fit that either without a special part. Overall, I am disappointed. I had automatically assumed bike racks were universal and did not realize that was not the case. I also did not realize that there is a chart that can be consulted to check for fit. That was my mistake.

Despite this, based on what I have noticed with this rack, the instructions are not very good. Both my boyfriend and I tried to figure them out and found them confusing. In addition, neither one of us believe this would fit three bikes unless the top rod was fastened all the way out and I doubt one would have that option on every car. Had this worked on my car, I would have given this three stars based on my other observations.
text_fidelity_b: Graber Guardian 3 Bike Trunk Rack

text_fidelity_a:
Cilkus Bicycle Pump with Pressure Gauge. Mini Portable Bicycle Pump Compatible with Presta and Schrader Valve Bicycles, Including air Bag Needle and Free Puncture Repair I had a tiny little hand pump and a giant full sized floor pump. I needed something to ride along with my on my bike. So I chose to go with a CO2 canister and this mini floor foot pump. When I saw how small it was, I didn't think it was going to be that effective. Especially with the tires that I'm blowing up. I'm running 26x4 fat tires and there's a lot of volume going on in there. Hopefully, I'll be moving to smaller tubes once I install some tannus armor. In the mean time, I needed more volume than the hand pump could provide and a something more portable than the floor pump.
I tested this out by dropping a tire from 30PSI to 20PSI. The chuck went on solid and locked without issue. The good news is that this pump does move air. The fact that I could see the needle move on the pressure gauge was a good indication of effectiveness. The none gauge version would have been nice for portability, but being able to read pressure on the fly is pretty necessary for me. Also the pump retainer/ foot hold works great for stabilizing the pump.

Things that don't work for me. I don't like that the hose comes out the side. It makes in harder to store.
I would have a like a pressure bleeder valve. And most importantly, the chuck leaks with taking it off. So you have to add more pressure than you planned on and you'd need another gauge that doesn't bleed to read the pressure afterwards.

Overall, while it could use some improvement, it's still a great little tool to have in an emergency. Or even if you want to soften the tires for off road and then pump them back up for the asphalt.
text_fidelity_b: Cilkus Bicycle Pump with Pressure Gauge. Mini Portable Bicycle Pump Compatible with Presta and Schrader Valve Bicycles, Including air Bag Needle and Free Puncture Repair

Coleman 3000000455 Latern Pump Kit This kit is dog easy the second time around. Unfortunately the second time may be decades away. Hopefully.
I faithfully disassembled my pump from my 45 year old Coleman stove (Bless em! Most of the guys who built the thing are no doubt long gone to their various rewards)....but anyway, I elected to rebuild the old pump which was a mistake. The new cup is designed for the new rod. It does not work on the old one.
On the old rod there is a metal stop that holds the cup. The new cup is different. If you have a super oldie like mine you will take the metal retaining clip off the new pump with needle nosed pliars. Wiggle under the metal clip and wiggle it off. Slide everything off. Put the round metal ring thingy which holds it to the tank on, then the spring. Follow with the NYLON stop ring. Then put the cup on top of that followed by the new round metal spring clip, or the old. That much is the same.
Put it back in the unit. I started it at the bottom and chased it around with my thumbnail until all of the cup was in....then shoved it home. Some people might have elected to put a bit of grease on the cup before installation but I chose the venerable 3-1 oil before...and after.
After all that it worked like a charm. It's quick and simple if you do it right.
text_fidelity_b: Coleman 3000000455 Latern Pump Kit

text_fidelity_a:
Light & Motion Vis 360 Plus Bike Helmet Light I commute by bike and I'm obsessed with seeing and being seen at night. I have a 650 lumen TerraLUX TT-5 flashlight (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009WFA4KU/) strapped to my handlebars as my primary light. I added this helmet-mounted light set as redundancy / extra security. I've had it about a month now.

This is a pretty good light. It's fairly bright, and I like that it has amber LED's on both sides of both the front and rear light. This makes you visible from any angle (hence the "360" in the name). Having gotten used to the blinding, virtual daylight of the 650 lumen flashlight on my handlebars, the 250 lumens that this light puts out on max doesn't seem quite bright enough to me. But I could get home safely with this alone if my flashlight were to fail, so it's bright enough.

Things I like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) You can aim the light wherever you need it. It's handy for checking out turns before you've made the turn. And I can now see the display from my bike computer without having to wait for a streetlight! And when I'm off my bike, I can see my lock, into my trunk bag, etc.
2) They increase visibility and therefore safety.
3) You'll probably leave them mounted to your helmet most of the time, so you're less likely to forget them. And if you're locking your bike up somewhere you'll probably take your helmet with you, so you'll automatically take your lights too - less chance of theft.

Things I like about this light in particular:
1) It's one of the brighter ones available.
2) It actively aims LED's in every direction, making you highly visible.
3) It's rechargeable and charges via USB.

Things I don't like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) They add weight to your head / neck.
2) They can get knocked around. I take my bike on the train for a portion of my commute, and when we near my stop I have my helmet on and am ready to get my bike out of the rack to disembark; meanwhile other riders are trying to get to their bikes. I frequently bang one or the other of the lights on the overhand above the bikes while we're all jostling around. Also, when I take my helmet off I feel I have to be more careful about stowing it so the lights don't get knocked about.

Things I don't like about this light in particular:
1) It's surprisingly heavy, and it's unbalanced. The front light is virtually weightless. The rear light, which has the battery pack, is surprisingly heavy. I invested in a very nice, "barely there" helmet that weighs virtually nothing. This light makes it feel like a brick. Obviously it's not that heavy, but it is heavier than I expected. And I don't like that all the weight is to the rear. This is okay when I'm leaning forward in riding position, but when I'm stopped at a light or otherwise upright, the weight is pulling my head back.
2) I find the rubberized button to turn it on / change modes difficult to feel and manipulate while I'm riding. If I don't take the train home, my commute is an hour and 15 minutes. To save battery I have it on low when I'm riding on well-lit streets and switch to high otherwise. I've had this light almost a month and I'm not getting better at feeling / adjusting the light. It takes concentration away from riding while I fiddle with it.
3) The tail light mode is not adjustable. It does this odd, slow fade-in / fade-out and that's it. You can't make it be always on, and you can't make it actually flash.
4) You can't have just the taillight on. Once the headlight's on, you can turn the taillight off independently, but you can't ride with just the taillight.
5) The battery is not replaceable. My flashlight / headlight runs on a replaceable, rechargeable battery, which means I can keep a spare battery in my pouch and be sure I have enough battery to get home. I can also ride with one battery while the other's at home recharging. With this light, if the battery runs out you can't use the light until you get to a USB charger. And it takes a good few hours to recharge, so you can't go riding for the hours it takes to recharge. And the low battery indicator is tucked away at the bottom of the taillight, and is only visible after you've plugged it in to recharge, so that doesn't help. So you'd better keep it charged.
6) You can change the angle of the front light, but only in discrete clicks. Each click is a very small angle of change on the device, but changes where the light hits the road by about 20'. I frequently want the light right in between two of the clicks and I can't put it there.
7) The helmet mounts strike me as odd. The front light slides into it's mount and clicks in place, but it slides in from the bottom. That means the if the clicky thing ever fails the light will slide out. If it slid in from the top gravity would keep it in place. And the rear light presses on with four tabs clicking into four slots. You really have to pull on it to dismount it. Odd.

Hmmm. Looking at this review there are way more things in the "don't like about this light" section than elsewhere, which makes it seem like I don't like this light. That's not true. None of the "don't likes" are show-stoppers. I'm keeping the light and I do like it. They're mostly just areas where I feel like the light could be somewhat better. If you buy this light you'll definitely be seen, you'll see where you're going, and you'll probably be happy you have it. These are just my observations for whatever they may be worth to you.
text_fidelity_b: Light & Motion Vis 360 Plus Bike Helmet Light

text_fidelity_a:
JOROTO X2 Stationary Exercise Bike | X2PRO Bluetooth Magnetic Belt Drive Indoor Cycling Bike, 300 Pounds Loads Fitness Cycle Bikes The UPS deliveryman carried this box to the front door with ease, but I quickly learned that a 108 lb., smooth, cardboard box is NOT that easy to maneuver. So just be aware this is a heavy shipment!

I was worried this was going to be a cheap and flimsy bike, but that's not the case in any way! This thing is welded, heavy gauge steel with a thick paint job (probably not powder coated). The handles are equally solid with a thick rubber grip, probably hot dipped. Basically, no amount of sweaty hands are going to cause the grip to deteriorate. The mechanics are practically silent.

Assembly is a cinch. There are 4 bolts used to attach the feet, three adjustable handles to attach the seat and handle, and two pedals to screw on. All of the required tools are in the box.

I've only ridden on it once, but the seat is soft (not that it matters if you're standing). The electronic display is of utmost cheapness, though. I was afraid that I was going to break it when installing the (included) AA batteries. It provides very basic information such as time, distance, "speed", and "calories" but there is no input for height and weight.

I'm waiting on a cadence sensor that will attach to one of the crank arms, and plan to use that with an app to get better feedback on pace. I also downloaded the Peloton app (30 day free trial) and was able to follow along just fine with the beginners ride. The resistance knob doesn't have a numeric scale (just +/-) so you'll have to judge for yourself based on how it feels.

Final thought is regarding the maneuverability. The front wheels are a bit small and made of a hard plastic so it will be hard to roll across carpet. You can tell from the photo we have a hard floor, and if it gets caught on debris, it may easily get stuck or scratch the floor.

Overall, I'm impressed with the build quality, assembly and performance. Only negatives are the ultra cheap display, lack of any integrated wireless technology (BYO), and the small wheels to move it around.
text_fidelity_b: JOROTO X2 Stationary Exercise Bike | X2PRO Bluetooth Magnetic Belt Drive Indoor Cycling Bike, 300 Pounds Loads Fitness Cycle Bikes

TiTo High Strength Titanium Alloy Tent Stakes Tent pegs Nail pegs for Canopy Camping Tent Dia 8mm and Length 240mm only 56G (8x300mm) These are the beefiest, most heavy duty titanium tent stakes I've ever seen. It is kind of overkill, making these out of titanium when a good chromoly steel of the same weight would be nearly as good. I'm sure a company could make quality steel stakes (albeit a little thinner) that would be just as strong, but I'm digressing, when you go premium, go big, go really big! And these are that.

Unfortunately the listing is kind of messed up and ambiguous. When I received them, as I hoped these are the stakes that are 8mm in diameter and 300mm in length. They are also around 70 grams a piece, not the lighter weight which my understanding is for a shorter version. I was anticipating the extra weight since another reviewer gave meaningful and helpful feedback. I completely understand and agree with the criticisms expressed about the heavy weight and the high cost. I also don't think these are good for backpacking, possibly could work for staking down heavier things like EzUps or large canopies. These are SOLID and reflect that fact with heavy weight. I don't mind that they weigh a lot because I only plan to use two of these stakes for setting up a secure ridgeline across poles, with lighter weight stakes for the guylines.

The cordage loops at the end seem kind of cheap and low quality in comparison to the stakes themselves. The stake materials, welds and finishing all look great, although a couple stakes new-out-of-the-package have a slight curve/bend to them. There are no sharp edges or other apparent issues. Overall I'm very pleased.
text_fidelity_b: TiTo High Strength Titanium Alloy Tent Stakes Tent pegs Nail pegs for Canopy Camping Tent Dia 8mm and Length 240mm only 56G (8x300mm)

text_fidelity_a: Nordic Track GX 4.2 Pro Exercise Bike I bought this bike to upgrade after purchasing the GX2.0 last year, which I had been completely delighted with.  I am so glad that I didn't order this bike first, because the seat is SOOOO uncomfortable, that I had to purchase a sheepskin seat cover just to ride it!  The description on this page as I am writing says, "...features an adjustable, oversized cushioned seat," which is completely untrue!!!  The seat is HARD!!!  The front edges of the narrow part of the seat are sharp, and when I first sat on it, I could feel them scraping my thighs so much I couldn't ride it.  I planned to give my GX 2.0 bike (with its VERY comfortable seat) to my daughter when I got the new one, and was glad I had not, so I could continue my daily riding.  Even with the sheepskin cover installed, this seat is way too hard, and I am going to have to purchase some cushioned biking shorts in order to be as comfortable as I was on the other bike.  I had been riding up to 71 minutes (for a 61 year old woman who hated to exercise, that was great), and today I was only able to ride 30 minutes.  I wish that NordicTrack offered other seats that one could purchase for this bike.  It was really a disappointment in that respect. I am hoping that the company will fix this terrible seat, and put the same one on that I had on my original bike!  All in all, it will most likely cost me another $100.00 for the sheepskin cushion and bike shorts I will have to get.
text_fidelity_b: Nordic Track GX 4.2 Pro Exercise Bike

text_fidelity_a:
Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit We do a lot of camping and living outdoors, and something we enjoy is easy to make food when we are outdoors. We look for ways to keep the cooler, extra stoves, skillets, dutch ovens and cast iron at home. I think we found our answer in Mountain House freeze dried entrees.

We purchased the Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit. In it we chose the Beef Stroganoff and took it to a scout meeting to try. During the scout meeting we talked about light weight backpacking as well as food options for emergency food at home.

After we boiled two cups of water we poured it into the pouch and zip locked it for 8 minutes. The contents where stirred and then served to many hungry scouts at the meeting. Every scout got a sample to try and a lot of them were hesitant. The overall surprise on their faces was priceless. They liked it and said it tasted great.

They wanted a pouch of the Beef Stroganoff for themselves. The scouts were surprised how easy the meal was to make and how simple the cleanup is. We did also like the zip lock feature not only for the re-hydrating process but also to keep the uneaten food for later if needed. They were also coming up with ways to reuse the pouch for other needs in the forest or on the trail to keep from throwing the empty pouch away.

Most of the scouts have never re-hydrated food or eaten MREs before. They were impressed with the ease of cooking and how lightweight it is to add to your day pack or back pack.

For camping, outings or emergency preparedness I would recommend Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit to have on hand. For one it has a long shelf life, for two you won’t starve as the contents of each pouch will satisfy a hungry kid or adult. A very tasty meal…especially in the middle of the forest!

Our only complaint (and the reason we deducted a star) is not all the water absorbed into the food, so it was very runny. The pack instructed to use 2 cups of water and I feel that was too much.
text_fidelity_b: Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit

text_fidelity_a:
MIAODAM Exercise Wheel and Resistance Band Ordered these for my son who’s struggled through quarantine to get an appropriate work out.. I know, I know- we’re all singing the same sad quarantine song (some in better tune than others-ha-ah!) This was an all inclusive workout set sold at a decent price point and although we had high hopes it would be as great as our gym membership.. (yeah, right!! We all need realistic expectations ..) this had its perks and drawback- ultimately, I would have liked to rate it 3.5 star. I would suggest this is set mean for beginners/novice level exercise enthusiast.. and could meet those needs fairly well. (Used 2-3x week and for 15-30min. at a time..) However, this might fall short for those expecting a little more from their equipment..

If purchasing keep in mind:

-The grip handles are smaller than some adult male hands..(at least in our house!) Obviously, this could prove problematic if.. ones grip is compromised right from the start. However, an adult females hand seems to fit the grip without issue.

-As with any elastic band the stretch is tighter when you begin. This set offers varied resistance (clearly marked by color) after x30 day use.. Lower resistance bands are showing more signs of “slack.” (Nothing has snapped on us! But, the lesser band is much easier to pull.. and I would beg to differ it’s because we’re getting so much stronger!!) Higher levels still have plenty of resistance but, we haven’t used nearly as much so, they stretch out - just something to keep in mind.

-Protect door jam with extra padding!! As these are braced against “wood” with a soft rounded ball, we have found- not all door jams are created equal (i’m pretty sure our door jams are made of wood composite?!!) So, be careful and add a small cut out of foam, washcloth or dish towel.. Anything you can easily rig to buffer The wall and protect it- bc, we noticed small indents being left on the door jam itself- not what we wanted and overtime without protection… It’ll only get worse!

-Appreciate the bag this came with to store all the items in along with the extra straps/gadgets. This does have instructions- however, they’re a bit tricky to read- just know you can Google a “how to video“ and obtain the info. easily enough . Would have loved to see this set contain added buffer pad for walls.. even a few photos with instructions- possibly something included in the future? I’d also appreciate including a magic eraser for the walls! The black rubber can leave small markings… Yes! These easily come off with wall eraser- Hence, the perk of including one in the bag!

Overall, this is not a bad set up. It can give a person- a good resistance workout.. It just has a few idiosyncrasies to work around.. I suggest knowing your audience and their physical size and ability… If, you do prior to any ordering- and are sure to protect the physical structure of the door when setting up- then, one should get what you need from this workout set.

I hope this info helps… Feel free to let me know!
text_fidelity_b: MIAODAM Exercise Wheel and Resistance Band

That aside, this is an air mattress that can hold some serious weight and not lose any air. That's amazing given some nightmare experiences that I've had.

text_fidelity_a:
cycmoto Anne Kids Bike for Toddlers and Kids, 14 16 Inch Girls Bike for 3-7 Years Old with Training Wheels and Basket, Pink, Yellow The bike arrived in good shape. Nothing was dented up and it was a reasonably smooth assembly. The tires arrived with enough air to get a few test rides in, but I wouldn't assume this to always be true and you will need to add air to the tires.

The listing states a novice can assemble this bike in 15 minutes. Unless you assemble bikes for a living it will take you longer than 15 minutes. However, this is the second bike I've assembled lately and the cycmoto was definitely easier. It will take you about 10 minutes just to unbox and remove all the foam and plastic ties. Then you will want to spend at least 10 minutes skimming through the instructions to brief yourself on the tasks at hand. I spent about 20 minutes getting all the necessary pieces together and partially tightened. Then I spent another 30 minutes adjusting, straightening, leveling and right sizing the seat, handlebars and brakes. You will want to refer to the instructions when adjusting the front brake. I did not install the training wheels, the basket or the splash guards (see comments below). So, if you just plan to assemble just the main pieces you should expect to spend about 75 minutes. If you plan to install all the extras then you should add another 30 minutes.

It comes with a flat metal multi tool and a dual size Allen wrench that can be used to completely assemble. I used the included tools to assemble. It was a little difficult for certain bolts, but it can be done. The only additional tool I used that was not included was a simple Phillips head screwdriver.

You should note that this bike has front and back hand brakes and not a coaster brake (if you pedal backwards it will spin backwards freely and not brake). The front brake (right handlebar) has two pads that squeeze the wheel to stop. The back brake (left handlebar) has a different stopping mechanism that is build into the crank system. The one concern I have with the brakes is that they are plastic. I hope they don't crack or break if the bike falls. Learning to use the hand brakes early could be better if you think the kid will grow into a mountain or bmx style bike.

A few things to note:

1) the instructions did not include a section for installing the splash guards. I am fairly confident I know which guard goes in the front/back by looking at the pictures in the listing. It would have been nice to have this in the instructions.

2) there are instructions for installing the basket, but I am either missing parts (the plate, small metal sheets and screws) or the instructions should be updated to describe attaching the basket using a ziptie like piece that was included. Personally, I would like to attach the basket as described in the instructions, but those parts were not included.

I did not install either the basket or splash guards. These are advanced attachments that should be used for kids who already know how to ride a bike with two wheels or if you plan to use training wheels. If you are purchasing this bike to train someone how to ride without training wheels then you should assume there will be a fall or two. By waiting to attach the splash guards and the basket you will avoid damaging while practicing to learn to ride a bike.

I would recommend not using the training wheels at all because it could make training without them more difficult. However, uou can adjust the height of the training wheels. So, if you start with the training wheels completely on the grown then you can slowly raise them off the ground.

Overall, the bike looks nice and feels solid.

This bike is made in China and being sold by Chinese company on Amazon.
text_fidelity_b: cycmoto Anne Kids Bike for Toddlers and Kids, 14 16 Inch Girls Bike for 3-7 Years Old with Training Wheels and Basket, Pink, Yellow

text_fidelity_a:
Thule Apex XT Bike Hitch Rack We are so impressed with this bike rack. It's nicer than any other that we have seen. It includes tools to help with assembly, but my husband chose to use his own adjustable wrench and socket set. It comes in 2 main pieces. You put those pieces together before installing it on your vehicle. There's a pin that is used to connect the 2 pieces. It did give my husband a little trouble at first when trying to push the pin in, but then he noticed that it was more like a bolt and threaded, so he used his socket set and screwed it in and that worked very well.

The next issue we had was putting the rack onto the receiver. There's a knob on the base of the rack that you tighten to lock it in to the receiver. You have to use the key to engage the knob in order to get it to work. At first, we didn't figure that out and it was hard to get it into the receiver and back out. In hindsight, it makes a lot of sense. Without the key, it can't be removed from the car so it can't be stolen. The instructions showed the key and knob, but there were only pictures, so we didn't really understand what it was getting at. Some verbal instructions would have helped with that.

Once the rack is installed, it doesn't budge. It's very sturdy and extremely well designed. We have a Toyota Sienna and you can swing the rack (with bikes) completely out of the way so you can open the trunk. That's a pretty cool feature! There are plenty of straps included to secure the bikes in place. The manual didn't show how to hang a women's bike, so we had to look online to figure out how to do that. There's also a cable lock that prevents the bikes from being removed from the rack without the key. That wasn't something we figured out right away either. That's another item where an explanation would have been helpful.

Overall, we are very happy with this. It is nicer than we expected and we highly recommend this.
text_fidelity_b: Thule Apex XT Bike Hitch Rack

text_fidelity_a:
Nathan Unisex Hydration Back-Pack for Running, Hiking, Cycling and more. 2L Bladder Included / 6L Storage Capacity. Adjustable Straps. NO BOUNCE while Running. I purchased this vest 6 years ago and it served me well in multiple ultras. It has just enough space for everything you need. I just checked the front zip pocket and it's just a tad too small for my Samsung Galaxy S7 Active, which is a thick phone. It definitely wouldn't fit an iPhone 6-7 Plus. The pack rides low enough on your back that there are no real issues with rubbing or chafing of the neck...from the pack. I did get a bit annoyed from time to time by the hose rubbing my neck, though. The side straps....what can I say? Over 6 years, I've never figured out how to adjust them well, lol. But it hasn't seemed to matter much. For a while, I used to over-cinch the chest strap but realized it can stay pretty loose and the pack is still not very bouncy. The front right pocket is where I've always tucked my phone. Although I admit sometimes I've used a SpiBelt with this pack to free up more pocket space for gels. You don't get a whole lot of space in the back pocket but it's perfect for those rarely used but "just in case" items I like to bring like an emergency poncho, extra sunscreen, lip balm, ginger chews, etc.

The bite valve on Nathan's bladder tube has always been problematic for me. I never really "bit" it hard yet within a year or so, it began to leak. After one race, my leg was covered in syrupy goo where gatorade and leaked and evaporated over the course of 50 miles. I swapped it out for the bite valve from a Camelbak and never had another problem. Like all bladders, be religious about cleaning this one post-use or it will gunk up very quickly. The closure system on the bladder takes some getting use to. You'll become a pro at it but for years I watched aid station volunteers stare in bewilderment, trying to figure out how to open it. More often than not, I ended up doing it myself.

I used to find after 100 milers that the top of my back would have a slightly chaffed feel to it, without anything being rubbed raw. I'm sure a light application of body glide or vasoline would have prevented that. But overall, this is a great, basic vest with plenty of fluid capacity. I recently replaced mine with Nathan's VaporAir, mainly for more pockets. But I could easily have bought this again and been happy.
text_fidelity_b: Nathan Unisex Hydration Back-Pack for Running, Hiking, Cycling and more. 2L Bladder Included / 6L Storage Capacity. Adjustable Straps. NO BOUNCE while Running.

text_fidelity_a:
Chase 8 Bike Hydration Vest - Integrated Tool Organization - 70 oz I traded out a perfectly good riding hydration pack made by another company to go with Camelbak, which is a company I very much like. I have a different pack ready to go for each of my major outdoor hobbies. This one for biking, of course.

One negative is that the other brand actually had an easier to fill, empty, and dry hydration pack. For some reason, Camelbak keeps changing theirs, and not always for the better: this one no longer has the little plastic pieces that flip out from around the circular fill area which - on my other recent models - helped the reservoir to drain and dry out easier. Since this does not have that feature, it stays flat, making it harder to dry, and it still has the rib inside the pack which keeps you from reaching in all the way to dry it out with a towel. All that said, the other-branded pack had a bit of a goofy tube that could kink and never quite looked or felt right.

But...another negative for the Camelbak - the reservoir from the other branded-pack came with a mouthpiece cover, whereas I have to buy yet another for use with this Camelbak. That should just come with because ...well, I've just been in too many disgusting places to not want to ensure my mouthpiece is covered. Even though the mouthpiece has changed, it does seem that the same covers will fit.

Weight and comfort are about perfect on this thing. And it holds what I need it to. Here is how I ride: In the front mini-compartment with the odd closure, I keep the stuff that's sort of permanent and hopefully I won't need often - my bike multi-tool, some small stuff to fix tires, and a spare tire. Also some sealing bags to put my phone and wallet in should it rain.

The main compartment I keep my tire pump, as my last pack had a spot for it and I like that better than having more crap on my actual bike. Also biking gloves. The other day, I comfortably had my sunglasses case and coffee mug in there as well.

I had the 2l reservoir almost full with all this. It was full, but totally fine. I also used the "stretch pocket" for my very compact wind-breaker once it was all wet and dirty, but I was too hot to wear it.

In the front zip pocket, I kept my keys and phone. Great place for them, since I compulsively check for them and this also allows for access to your phone if you need to take a pic or something. I would have liked a specific latch or zip pocket for keys...it does have net pocket for that that seems appropriate, but a zipper would be better. I don't want to worry there is any possibility such a thing could slip out.

I also keep my biking GPS in the other mesh pocket when it's not on my bike.

Once you get the straps just how you need them (and note that you may have to adjust them if you add or subtract a lot of gear), this pack manages to feel so streamlined that it is almost a part of you. It's up high on your back and tight against you all around. No air channels in the back except for some minor mesh, so it stays light and streamlined. 2 front straps built in keep a nice grip without a lot of extra straps getting in the way.

Although it says unisex, I'm not sure this is great for women. I know a lot of women's Camelbaks have straps built a certain way to avoid breasts, but these are all over my chest, so I'm not sure it would be comfortable for a woman (but I really wouldn't know).

Also, I'm not sure if huge dudes could wear this comfortably. I am ~73.5", 185 lbs., and I have my chest straps about as loose as they can be made, although I have a bit of room left on the back straps. It's hard for me to tell how far that will go in the chest area.

The zippers and seams are well hidden making this great for people who want a sleek and simple design, while still being of obvious quality.

It also seems to be water resistant, as none of my stuff got wet the other day in a brief but heavy rain.

The only thing that had bothered me while riding was the tube was noticeable behind my head. But now I just realized the tube can go in either side, so that point becomes moot!

Overall, an excellent pack. Perfect for my half-day biking needs.
text_fidelity_b: Chase 8 Bike Hydration Vest - Integrated Tool Organization - 70 oz

text_fidelity_a:
Black Diamond Revolt Headlamp Everyone I know uses Black Diamond headlamps, but I've always owned Petzl. I've always wondered if I'd like BD better. When I had a bag stolen that had my newest Petzl headlamp in it I thought I'd try out the Black Diamond Revolt. For a headlamp that can recharge batteries with a USB cable it was a really good price, so I pulled the trigger on it. It has adequate lumens for my purposes (backpacking, evening hiking, and use around the house), although it isn't quite as bright as my similarly priced Petzl models. It has an awesome, fully adjustable dimmer setting that is the one thing that stands out as better than any other headlamp I've used. It also has a red LED setting, which is important to me - I actually find that I use the red LED way more than the white for late night use. As far as features go, I'm happy with everything you get with the Revolt.

The more I've used this headlamp though, I have a few minor complaints compared to similar offerings from Petzl. As mentioned above, I use the red LED setting often. It's great when you want to maintain night vision. I also like that if I wake up in the middle of the night and quickly use my lamp, the red LED wakes me up less than a bright white light. The problem for me is that the red setting on the Revolt is way too dim. It's hard to see anything that's more than just a few feet away. This makes it so that I can't use it in as many situations as I could with my old Petzl. I definitely wish it were brighter in the red mode.

Another feature on most headlamps is an adjustable angle setting where you can click it up and down to choose how high the lamp points. The Revolt has solid detents that seem like they will hold up well over time. This is kind of splitting hairs, but I don't like how widely spaced the detents are. It always seems to be too high or too low. YMMV, but I liked Petzl again here for the finer adjustments. I have to fiddle with the Revolt more often.

On the other hand, I'm not gentle with my headlamps. I use them constantly at home and work and any time I backpack or travel. I cram them into bags, toss them around a bit, bump them on things and occasionally drop them. It's hard to say, but friends that I work with and backpack with seem to have better luck with their Black Diamond lamps' durability. The Revolt is solidly built and seems to use batteries very efficiently. It seems like it might be a little sturdier and maybe last longer than my previous Petzl lamps, but that's purely a guess at this point. We'll see, but so far so good. I'm basing that more on friends' experiences with BD lamps. Either way, it's certainly no worse.

Overall, I think this is a pretty good headlamp. It's a solid value for the price and does everything I want it to. I'll continue to use it pretty happily, but when it comes time to replace it, I'll go back to Petzl. Even if the Revolt is a little sturdier, I like the way Petzl lamps work and feel. They're less clunky and they just seems to have their headlamps really dialed across the board. They're comfortable, intuitive and very well designed. Get a Revolt if you want a solid, functional headlamp, but get a Petzl if you really want to love it.
text_fidelity_b: Black Diamond Revolt Headlamp

Honestly, I wasn't expecting much. However, this little unit worked incredibly well.

It charges quickly via USB Micro (120 minutes to full charge / with 30 inflates per charge), has all of the accessories needed to get going (USB cable, air needles, attachment hose, etc..), has pre-set modes for a football, a soccer ball, a basketball, etc.. And is super compact & lightweight (6.29" x 1.4" & weighing only 6.5oz).

I haven't tried, but don't see why you couldn't even inflate a bicycle tire with this unit as well. However, I probably wouldn't try with anything larger like a car or truck tire out of concern of damaging the pump.

There is an auto-shut off option (IE: when you use a ball preset the pump will turn off when it dispenses the appropriate amount of air for the selected ball), however, there is no pressure gauge. So, if you don't use the preset, then you have to go by feel (or have an air gauge on hand).

As far as my experiment, I didn't even use the presets. Just popped in the needle into my slam ball & turned on the pump. It inflated (my very deflated) slam ball in a matter of seconds. A success!

If you're constantly using a foot pump or bike pump to inflate your sports equipment, bike tires, etc.., then seriously consider this portable pump instead. Makes this process super easy. There's even an attachment that looks like it's to be used for blowing up balloons! Very cool!

text_fidelity_a:
Rhode Gear Highway 2 Bike Rack This brand is a subsidiary of Yakima and has a 3 year warranty. You don't get the bells and whistles, but for $55 delivered, who cares? It's built solid and I like being able to bolt it into the receiver with the threaded bolt/pin--makes it more stable. Any hitch mount like this has to have a wide tolerance range due to different hitch designs (ours is an '07 4Runner 2"). If someone has a wrench they could remove the vertical bar of any tilt model like this anyway, so I'm not concerned about not being able to use a locking pin on it.

As for the velcro straps, if you rub them in when fastening they seem just ok, but there is an included extra strap that you can do a figure-eight with around the bike tubes and top carrier bars for extra security. I'm fully confident that I could do a multi-state road trip with our two bikes on this with no problem. You could always replace the straps later too as they just go through and around the rubber holder.

I use bungee cords to hold the wheels, pedals, and bikes to each other.

Price/Performance it gets 5 stars from me.
text_fidelity_b: Rhode Gear Highway 2 Bike Rack

I love fishing. There's nothing I'd rather do on the whole world. Nothing. You know what I mean... Lol! I've been fishing for decades, but have only been fly fishing for 3 years or so. I have several spinning rods in the $100-$200 range, and they are amazing. Unfortunately a $200 fly rod isn't the same as a $200 spinning rod. You can easily spend $3000 on a high end fly rod!

Well, I don't want to. I don't think it's necessary. But I've been fishing long enough that I can feel a great rod when I handle one. That's good, because I've seen lots of very expensive rods that were trash, and a few hidden gems that punched WAY above their weight. The Maxcatch Premiere line is one of those hidden gems. I picked this 3WT up just to check out, and after I effortlessly my fly 55' and landed it precisely where I wanted it. Over and over again. I mean it is so accurate that it's almost boring lol! And it's a $55 rod!

The blank is very sensitive, very light, very well finished and attractive, and the cork and dark chromed accents are beautiful. I'm surprised at how nice the cork is at this price point!

So I fish. A lot. I used to sell fishing equipment for a living, and I've handle a lot of gear. Is this Maxcatch a Loop or high end Sage? No. But it's also not $400-$900. However, I'd put this up against ANY Reddington, Fenwick, or lower end Sage any day and put money on the Maxcatch.

Get this rod. You'll be glad you did. You'll catch a ton of fish if you do your part, because this is a magnificent tool at an amazing price!

EDIT: I caught that monster 'Bow on the 4wt. Great fight! The rod was bent in half for 5 minutes, and held up great. And I felt every run, head shake, and dive. Great rods!

text_fidelity_a:
Eco Vessel Summit Discontinued 2014 Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle with Flip Straw (17-Ounce, Blue Glow) I really loved these bottles at first, so much so that I bought 8 of them. They keep my water very cold for a long, long time and I like the lids (I use them without the straws). I can hook them onto whatever I need to help me carry them, as well.

Unfortunately, my love affair with these bottles has ended all too soon. The first thing I noticed is that the paint started coming off. The red one is the worst. The paint is flaking off to the point that it would be better off if I pull the rest of it off to turn it silver instead of blotched red. But I could have lived with that.

What got me was when I started to fill one up only to discover that the plastic ring around the top of the bottle that you use to screw the lid in has split. It split completely down. There was nothing I could do. It had to either go back to the manufacturer or the trash. Since I'm a grad student, the last thing I have is extra time so I put it in the trash.

I started checking my other bottles and discovered that the plastic ring was put on at a tilt on some of the bottles (based on the amount of space under the ring not being uniform on all bottles).

Then I looked at my other bottles and noticed that the Hydro Flask's ring was metal, not plastic. I like those bottles just as much, but had to buy the straw lids separately. However, now that I see the flaw in the Eco Vessel bottles, I'm going to start replacing them with the Hydro Flask brand. Not only are they completely metal (except the lid, of course), but the finish does not show signs that it will flake off.

All in all, the plastic ring used to screw the lid onto the bottle is a fatal flaw for these bottles.

UPDATE: I added pictures showing the paint flaking off and the warped plastic at the top. I did not take pictures of the one that broke, but I thought showing one that's not broken yet, but clearly warped, might be helpful.
text_fidelity_b: Eco Vessel Summit Discontinued 2014 Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle with Flip Straw (17-Ounce, Blue Glow)

text_fidelity_a:
Weslo Cadence R 5.2 Treadmill I've had this for a little while now. I'm short and overweight, and usually fail at my daily walking goals, BUT, I've been very pleased with this purchase. Being the aforementioned short and overweight, the preset workouts are just a bit much for me, but it wouldn't take too much work to get there, I don't think. Probably my favorite feature is its simplicity. A lot of people want bells and whistles and wouldn't be happy with this, but it's perfect for this not-athletic person. I'll never get up to the faster speeds, but to be honest, it shakes enough under my weight when I attempt a light jog, that I'd be just a little leery of pushing it any more. Otherwise it feels sturdy though, and I'm not afraid of it breaking or anything.

As others have said, a second set of hands really helps when putting it together initially. It's not hard, just awkward. My mom helped me by just holding things still or handing me parts. It maybe took a half hour from start to finish, and I was taking my time. Getting it exactly where I wanted in my small room was the hardest part. Folding it up is easy - it's heavy, but I'd be scared to use anything lighter!

This is my first treadmill, and I think it's perfect for a casual user. I doubt I'll ever be an avid walker/jogger, but this at least gives me ample opportunities for exercise when I need it, without worrying about time of day or weather.
text_fidelity_b: Weslo Cadence R 5.2 Treadmill

Fitbit Charge HR Wireless Activity Wristband (Tangerine, Large (6.2 - 7.6 in)) Best gift I've ever received. The day after I received this from my wife for Christmas, I set it up and entered my weight loss plan and set my goals. I've worn it every day since and followed the plan with will power and determination. My plan is simple: 1. Entered and tracked everything I ate to stay under my daily calorie intake goal, 2. Set a goal for steps per day and tried to achieve it every day. Started off modestly at 5000 steps per day and increased to 8000 as endurance increased and weight came off.
That's it! No complicated diet plan that takes too much time to figure out, keep track of and lose interest in after a few weeks of struggle. So, the only plan that worked for me is the one described above and the one we hear all the time. Watch what you eat and exercise. That's it! I've lost 52 pounds in seven months so it was a steady, healthy loss. My doc took me off my blood pressure meds two weeks ago because my blood pressure was a little too low. My cholesterol numbers went from high to the lower end of the normal range. I'm over 65 and feel better and have more energy than I've had in years. It takes some work, commitment and a lot of will power but I'm here to tell you that it can be done.
The device itself is fairly easy to set up and sync with your mobile phone. It gives you a lot of information about your daily activity and keeps track of your sleep and the food you eat (you have to enter the food type and quantity using their food data base). Once you get used to it you'll find that it doesn't take much time at all to make the entries for food intake by selecting them from the extensive Fitbit food data base. The Fitbit app builds up a little personal data base of the foods you eat frequently and most recently. It also lets you enter your own foods or meal if it's data base doesn't have it. You can also enter a food by scanning its bar code. Simple.
I know this sounds like a paid ad but I haven't received any compensation or product discount for my review. Just want to share my experience.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Charge HR Wireless Activity Wristband (Tangerine, Large (6.2 - 7.6 in))

Tresda Camping Lantern Rechargeable, 370LM Dimmable LED Vintage Battery Powered Lanterns, Waterproof LED Retro Camping Lights for Camping, Power Outages, Hurricane, Outdoors, Home Décor I'm very pleased with this camping light. The design mimics an old school lantern. To my eye is a far more attractive design than the typical LED lantern. The body is plastic, but it's a good quality plastic that has a nice, solid feel to it. The army green housing is nicely complemented with a bamboo surround on the base. The rope handle is functional and attractive. The cage and hanging points are metal. The USB charge port has a silicone cap to keep water/dirt out. The cap is tethered to the body so it won't get lost.

Controls are simple: a single knob that turns it on with a nice, solid click. It has a good dimmable range, from a soft night light level to a full room (or tent) level of light.

The best feature is that it uses standard 18650 Li-ion batteries. I am so tired of battery powered items that have non-removable batteries since, when the battery eventually fails, you have to toss the item. With this, you just have to replace the 18650 cells when they will no longer hold a charge well. Plus, since I always have charged 18650 cells for other items, when the batteries run down I don't have to wait for the lantern to charge -- just swap out the batteries for a freshly charged set and you're back in business.

The batteries can be charged without having to remove them (there's a USB C port on the lantern body with a single LED charge light indicator) but, as with any 18650, it's best to charge them in an external charger. The cells claim to be 2400 mAh, but that's somewhat optimistic -- I get a bit less than 2000 mAh capacity when I discharged and metered them. The internal charge rate is 0.6A -- a bit slow, but ideal for good battery longevity.

My only quibble is that I would have liked if the included batteries were from a major brand, such as Sony/Murata, Samsung or LG. But the ones included have been performing fine since an LED light is a pretty low-demand task for an 18650 cell.

A good performing, good looking light that you won't have to toss when the batteries reach their end of life. Five stars and a good value for the price.
text_fidelity_b: Tresda Camping Lantern Rechargeable, 370LM Dimmable LED Vintage Battery Powered Lanterns, Waterproof LED Retro Camping Lights for Camping, Power Outages, Hurricane, Outdoors, Home Décor

text_fidelity_a:
Black Diamond Distance FL Trekking Pole I love these poles with the exception of a few minor things.

I love how quickly i can 'fold' these up without losing my length setting. And I love how short they fold up, and I can put them under the compression straps of my day pack. They will even fit inside if need be. Swing weight is very lite and I have had zero issue with slipping. I love the little rubber tips, which are replacable if/when they wear out. I also like the minimal baskets to allow the sections to clip together.

The few things I wish were better
The straps are fiddly to adjust and are not particularly comfortable, but not enough to be a true negative. I wish the straps had the traditional 1/2 twist rather than the method they use to have the strap lay flat under your hand. While it works, I futz with it a lot. I hope the strap issue are minimized as I use them more and strap conform to my hands better.
The handle is a little bit small and I don't have particularly large hands. Could be an issue for people with larger hands. While not really an issue for me, I plan to wrap some tennis grip around the handle.
I wish the handle had a 'trigger'.

They click a bit when using them. But I guess that is the price to pay for the quick/short break down capability.
